comparator.name: Public Administration
comparator.sourceNotes: The live 2026-2027 Leiden Study Guide identifies three formal 180-EC Public Administration routes. The generic target is represented by Policy, Public Administration, and Organisation because it most broadly covers the programme's public-administration identity across policy, institutions, organisations, management, law, politics, sociology, economics and research methods; the choice is independent of UCR fit. The route totals 60 EC in each year. Years 1 and 2 each contain twelve compulsory 5-EC courses. Year 3 contains a 15-EC bachelor thesis, three compulsory 5-EC courses and 30 EC of genuine elective space. The zero-credit mentorship and legacy cohort-only modules are omitted. Current29creditbearingcomponents independently checked through individual2026moduleAPIs; mentorship0 is mandatory but outside180. The15ECthesis applies entrants from2022, with115eligibleEC and namedconditions established from currentcourse entry. B1/B2nominalcompletion120meets entry before standardB3springthesis. Optionalinternshipnotrequired;formalcohort-onlylegacy modulesnotcounted.

alternatives.concept: A broad public-administration programme examining how governments and public organisations make, justify and implement decisions. Political science, law, sociology, economics, leadership and communication are combined with quantitative and qualitative research and applied policy analysis.

alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum integrates politics, law, sociology, economics, organisational leadership, policy questions and mixed research methods around public institutions and decisions. The actual curriculum supports this combined emphasis; it does not reproduce Dutch administrative training or guarantee a completed independent public-administration thesis.

alternatives.concept: Focuses on how economic institutions, incentives, public finance, organisations and management shape government choices. Economics, accounting and econometrics are integrated with politics, law, sociology, strategy, leadership and qualitative research.

comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The generic Public Administration target does not name a route. Of Leiden's three current formal routes, Policy, Public Administration, and Organisation most broadly represents public administration through policy formation and implementation, public organisations and management, political and legal institutions, economics, mixed methods, leadership and a thesis. Economics, Public Administration, and Management and Digitalisation, Governance and Society are more specialised directions.

The target's current formal routes and direct interests independently support an economics-and-management programme and a digital-government, data and responsible-AI programme. All three concepts are coherent and feasible. The closest and economic routes differ by seven courses in each direction, the closest and digital routes by seven, and the economic and digital routes by eleven, so every pair exceeds the 30-EC distinctness floor. Three is the maximum.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both examine political institutions, democracy and different national political systems; UCR adds comparative empirical inquiry.

Both examine policy effectiveness, stakeholder interests and evaluation. UCR develops governance diagnosis and policy advice for sustainability issues, without reproducing the entire implementation/evaluation sequence.
Both develop sociological theories of institutions, inequality and social change relevant to governing society.
Both introduce microeconomic and macroeconomic reasoning about markets, incentives and public choices.
Both examine political authority, rights and competing normative visions of governing. UCR surveys political thought rather than a public-administration-specific treatment.
Both examine public authority through legal principles and institutions; UCR also surveys private law and social justice.
Both examine EU institutions, actors, legitimacy and policy processes.

International organisations and the legal rules governing cross-border collective action are a substantive common object. UCR emphasises international legal principles, rather than the full organisational study of international administration.
Both develop and apply ethical theories to questions of action and responsibility. UCR addresses general ethical problems rather than specialising in public officials and administrative institutions.

Both examine strategic persuasion, framing and public-facing communication. UCR applies these in community and municipal sustainability projects, rather than a dedicated lobbying and interest-representation course.

Both develop evidence-based policy reports about contested public problems. UCR uses conflict analysis, a policy brief and research dossier rather than Leiden’s group qualitative investigation of multi-level governance.

AI fairness, privacy, responsibility and political risk address an important part of governing digital technology. UCR is an AI ethics course; Leiden additionally studies public digital services, social media, data science and other government technology domains.
Both examine leadership, ethical judgment and communication. UCR uses leader interviews and an advisory report, rather than focusing exclusively on public leadership.

Both study constitutional powers and administrative constraints, including participation, remedies and procedural fairness. UCR is comparative rather than a dedicated Dutch constitutional and administrative law course.

Negotiating with stakeholders and handling power, conflict and relationships addresses an identifiable part of public managers’ outward and internal work. UCR does not reproduce the full public-management, financial or crisis-management curriculum.

Both examine policy-making phases, competing interpretations and public decisions. UCR uses a sugar-policy case across national and international arenas, rather than the same introductory policy-science syllabus.
Comparative politics and sustainability governance provide related institutional perspectives, but no selected course reproduces this integrated introduction to public administration as a discipline.
General modern sociology and political thought do not establish Leiden’s specific Dutch political-administrative history from around1650 to the present.
General ethics and political philosophy do not reproduce this component’s epistemology, scientific demarcation and foundations of public-administration knowledge.
Genuine open elective space has no predetermined substantive counterpart.
Both examine organisational structures, culture, leadership and behaviour; UCR approaches these through organisational psychology rather than exclusively public organisations.
Both examine public goods, market failure, taxation, spending and government intervention.

Both examine budgeting, costing, organisational control and investment decisions. UCR teaches accounting and corporate finance rather than the public budget cycle, intergovernmental finance and Dutch public-sector rules.
Both teach descriptive statistics, association, estimation and hypothesis testing for empirical research; UCR also integrates research design and a group project.
Both develop regression-based inference for social questions. UCR extends into econometric estimators and tests, rather than reproducing every public-administration application.
Both develop qualitative research design, interviews, coding, interpretation and reflexive inquiry; UCR is not restricted to public-administration applications.

Research design is substantively present within the UCR statistics and qualitative-methods courses, shown against their strongest respective counterparts. No separate selected course supplies this additional social-science foundations component.
Municipal communication and other applied projects do not establish the specific empirical investigation of responsive government and tailored public service in this required integrative project.
No scheduled course establishes a completed15ECindividual Public Administration thesis. Optional independent research is shown under the standard comparison rule outside scheduled180EC.

notes.text: Leiden provides a dedicated Public Administration sequence with route-specific policy, organisation, economics or digital-government courses and a 15-EC thesis. UCR can build three coherent 24-course programmes from politics, law, sociology, economics, leadership, data science, AI and research methods, but it does not reproduce the same continuous disciplinary sequence; shared rows indicate substantive overlap rather than full equivalence.

audience.programmeDescription: Public Administration examines how governments and public organisations make decisions, manage institutions and respond to societal problems. This comparison follows Leiden’s Policy, Public Administration and Organisation route, with dedicated policy, management, law and research training.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes approach public decisions through different combinations: policy and organisations; economics, accounting and management; or data, AI and public accountability. They offer substantive related study but do not reproduce Leiden’s continuous public-administration sequence, Dutch administrative history and law, integrative government projects or required individual thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The route totals 180 EC: 60 EC in each year, including 30 EC of open study and a 15-EC individual thesis. Thesis entry requires 115 eligible EC with specified methods and project requirements; minor, elective and internship credits cannot replace the required compulsory credits. First-year mentorship is mandatory without additional EC. Internships are optional and cannot coincide with the thesis.

componentNotes.bsk3-thesis: Required 15-EC individual empirical thesis. Entry requires a passed first year (60 EC), Quantitative Methods (5 EC), Qualitative Methods (5 EC), Integrative Project II (5 EC) and 40 EC of other compulsory later-year courses. Eligibility is checked on 1 August or 15 January; block-two resits do not count for spring entry. A thesis and internship cannot run concurrently.
componentNotes.bsk3-electives: 30 EC of open study, normally in the first semester of year three. Minor, exchange and elective approvals depend on the selection. Optional 15/30-EC internships require 90 earned programme EC including the first year, prior approval and 400/816 hours respectively.
componentNotes.bsk1-project: Required group research project with mandatory meetings, presentation and peer review. The exam and group paper must each pass.
